posts.title: Why we compare tiles at one o’clock
posts.excerpt: Yuka Brandt on the sun edge crossing the window bench, and why a tile is only judged once it has seen real light.
posts.content:
Shop lamps flatten glaze and stone. A matt porcelain that reads warm and pale at ten in the morning turns a cooler grey by four in the afternoon, and neither is wrong: both are the tile. That is why the low comparison bench in our showroom stands in the long south-east window, where the light changes by the hour and the materials show it.

The best comparing light falls between 10:00 and 14:00. Around 13:00 the sun edge crosses the bench, and for a few minutes two tiles lying side by side show their shade variation more honestly than any sheet can describe. Nadia Kowalczyk settled her kitchen floor in exactly that quarter hour.

We do not ask anyone to decide at the bench alone. Take samples home, lay them against your cabinet doors and paint, and look again at eight, noon and six. Then come back, or write to us, and we will turn the choice into a spec sheet, a layout drawing and a delivery.

posts.title: Reading a shade-variation code
posts.excerpt: Amira Haddad on V1 to V4, and why natural stone is nearly always V3 or V4.
posts.content:
Stone is never uniform, and it should not be. Amira Haddad reads every sheet against the physical sample before it goes out, and she explains shade variation in plain words: V1 is almost uniform, V4 varies a great deal from piece to piece.

Natural stone usually sits at V3 or V4, which is exactly what you want from a travertine wall and exactly what you need to know before ordering forty square metres of it. The code is on every spec sheet, next to the slip rating, so an architect can check both in one glance.

If you are unsure what a code means for your room, bring a plan or a photograph. Amira will lay out two samples at the different variations and let the daylight explain the rest.
